title: False Teachers and the God Who Rescues
summary: Peter warns that false teachers will arise in the church as false prophets arose in Israel, bringing destructive heresies, greed, and immorality. Three examples from Scripture (the angels who sinned, the flood, and Sodom and Gomorrah) show that God judges the ungodly and rescues the righteous. The rest of the chapter paints the teachers in stark images and warns that turning back after knowing the way of righteousness leaves a person worse off than before.
story: In chapter 1, Peter reminded his readers of the precious promises they had received and grounded the hope of Christ's coming in two witnesses: his own eyewitness experience of Jesus' transfiguration and the prophetic word of Scripture, which came from God and not from human will. Chapter 2 turns on that last point. Just as there were true prophets in Israel, there were false ones, and the church will have its counterfeits too. The chapter explains what those teachers are like and why their doom is certain. It prepares for chapter 3, where Peter answers the particular claim these teachers were making: that the Lord's promised coming would never arrive.
historical:
The letter presents itself as the last word of Simon Peter, written shortly before his death (1:14), which tradition places in Rome under Nero in the mid-60s AD. Its authorship is among the most debated questions in the New Testament. Many scholars regard 2 Peter as pseudonymous, written in Peter's name late in the first century or early in the second, pointing to its style, which differs from 1 Peter, its reference to a collection of Paul's letters (3:15-16), and its slow acceptance in the early church; Eusebius listed it among the disputed books. Others defend Petrine authorship, noting that a secretary could explain differences in style, that the letter's personal claims are specific, and that the early church ultimately rejected known forgeries while accepting this letter.

This chapter has an unusually close relationship with the letter of Jude. Jude 4-18 and 2 Peter 2:1-3:3 share many images in much the same order: the angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, slandering glorious beings, Balaam, waterless springs and clouds, blackest darkness, and the scoffers of the last days. Most scholars think 2 Peter adapted Jude; a smaller number argue that Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on a common source. Notably, 2 Peter leaves out Jude's direct use of 1 Enoch and the dispute over the body of Moses, and adds positive examples of rescue (Noah and Lot) that Jude lacks.
cultural:
The false teachers traded on a promise of freedom (verse 19). In the Greek world of the day, some philosophers taught that the gods did not intervene in human affairs or judge wrongdoing. The Epicureans, for example, held that the gods lived untroubled and unconcerned with humans, and that fear of divine punishment was a burden to be thrown off. Whether Peter's opponents drew directly on such ideas or not, their message sounds similar: there is no coming judgment, so the body's appetites can be followed without fear. Peter answers that God has judged before and will again.

Verse 4 uses the verb tartaroo, to cast into Tartarus. In Greek mythology Tartarus was the deepest pit of the underworld, lower than Hades, where the Titans who rebelled against the gods were imprisoned. Jewish writers of the period also used the word for the place where rebellious angels were held. Peter borrows a term his readers would recognize to describe the confinement of the angels who sinned, most likely the beings of Genesis 6:1-4 as that passage was read in Jewish tradition. Verse 13 mentions the teachers feasting with the church, a reference to the shared meals of early Christian worship, which Jude 12 calls love feasts.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1-3 announce the false teachers and their fate. Verses 4-10a form one long conditional sentence in Greek: if God did not spare the angels, if he did not spare the ancient world but preserved Noah, if he condemned Sodom and Gomorrah but rescued Lot, then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and hold the unrighteous for judgment. Each judgment is paired with a rescue, which gives the passage its comfort. Verses 10b-22 turn to vivid denunciation, a style found in Old Testament prophecy and in Jewish moral writing, with piled-up images: irrational animals, blots and blemishes, eyes full of adultery, springs without water, mists driven by a storm. The chapter closes with two proverbs, the first drawn from Proverbs 26:11.

outline.t: False teachers will come, as false prophets did
God judges the ungodly and rescues the righteous: angels, Noah, Lot
Arrogant, greedy, and following the way of Balaam
Empty promises of freedom and the danger of turning back

doctrines.note: God's judgment is not idle. The examples of the angels, the flood, and Sodom show that God holds the unrighteous for judgment, and that the delay of that judgment is not its cancellation (verse 3).

Alongside judgment runs rescue. God preserved Noah and delivered Lot, and the chapter's central claim is that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials (verse 9). Rescue comes in the middle of a corrupt world, not by removal from it.

Verse 1 speaks of the teachers denying the Master who bought them, using the language of a slave purchased by a new owner. It is one of the passages in the debate over the extent of the atonement, discussed below.

words.note: Tartaroo, to cast into Tartarus, used only here in the New Testament. It borrows the Greek name for the lowest region of the underworld, where rebels were imprisoned. Peter uses it for the holding place of the angels who sinned, awaiting final judgment. The word marks confinement before judgment rather than describing the final state.

Despotes, master or owner, the word for a slave's lord. Peter calls Christ the Master who bought them, picturing redemption as a purchase from one owner into the possession of another. The false teachers are rebels against the one who owns them by right.

Eleutheria, freedom. The teachers promise freedom, but Peter points out that a person is a slave to whatever masters him (verse 19). The New Testament's freedom is always freedom from sin for God; freedom offered as a license for appetite turns out to be a new slavery.

christ: Jesus is named in this chapter as the Master who bought his people (verse 1) and as our Lord and Savior (verse 20), knowledge of whom is the way people escape the corruption of the world. The chapter shows Christ as the rightful owner of those he has redeemed, and denial of him as the root of the false teachers' corruption. The paired stories of judgment and rescue also echo Jesus' own teaching: he compared the days before his coming to the days of Noah and of Lot, when life went on as normal until judgment fell (Luke 17:26-30). Peter follows his Lord in using these same examples as warnings to be ready.

hard.q: Do verses 20-22 teach that a true believer can lose salvation, and did Christ buy those who are finally lost?
hard.a:
The passage raises two linked questions that Christians have answered differently. On apostasy, Arminian and Wesleyan readers take verses 20-22 at face value: these teachers had truly escaped the world's corruption through knowing Christ and then fell away, showing that genuine believers can turn back and be lost. Calvinist and Reformed readers argue that the teachers had outward knowledge and association with the church but were never regenerated, and they point to the proverbs of verse 22: the dog and the pig return to what they always were, never having changed their nature.

On verse 1, those who hold that Christ died for all people see here clear evidence that he bought even those who deny him. Those who hold to particular redemption, that Christ died effectively for the elect, suggest that Peter describes the teachers as they presented themselves, or uses the language of ownership in a broad sense, of Christ's rightful claim over all who have professed his name. Both sides agree on the chapter's pastoral point: to know the way of righteousness and then walk away is spiritually devastating, and the warning is to be heeded, not merely debated.

questions: Peter's false teachers promised freedom but were themselves enslaved. What promises of freedom in your own world actually lead to a new kind of bondage?
The chapter pairs every judgment with a rescue. How does knowing that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly change the way you face a corrupt environment?
Greed appears twice as the false teachers' motive (verses 3 and 14). How can a church recognize when teaching has become a way of making money off people?
